body:
Meaning of safeguarding

Safeguarding refers to measures that ensure a living cultural tradition can continue to be practised, transmitted and developed by the people who maintain it.

Under Article 2(3) of the 2003 UNESCO Convention, safeguarding encompasses identifying and recording heritage, research, protection, preservation, promotion, education, transmission and revitalization.

Its ultimate purpose is the continued viability of the tradition. Maintaining a collection of historic objects or recordings is valuable, but does not by itself ensure that the associated cultural knowledge survives.

Bearer communities

Bearer communities consist of people who recognise, practise, maintain and transmit a living cultural tradition.

They may include artisans, religious practitioners, performers, musicians, storytellers, teachers, families and other participants. A bearer community is not necessarily confined to a single caste, religion, occupation or geographical settlement.

For example, the communities maintaining Garba include dancers, musicians, craftspeople and others involved in religious and festive activities.

Safeguarding should involve these communities in identifying the tradition, determining appropriate protection measures and managing its transmission.

Modes of transmission

ModeHow knowledge is transmitted
Family transmissionOlder relatives teach younger family members.
ApprenticeshipLearners acquire skills under experienced practitioners.
Community participationPeople learn through festivals, ceremonies and collective activity.
Oral transmissionKnowledge passes through narration, recitation and verbal instruction.
Formal educationSchools, institutions and organised courses teach relevant knowledge.
Non-formal educationWorkshops, community groups and practical learning support transmission.

Threats to living heritage

Intangible cultural heritage may become endangered when the conditions necessary for its continuation disappear.

  • Declining participation of younger generations.
  • Insufficient livelihood opportunities for practitioners.
  • Loss of raw materials or traditional cultural spaces.
  • Migration and social changes that disrupt transmission.
  • Displacement of traditional products by cheaper industrial substitutes.
  • Commercial pressures that distort the meaning or practice of a tradition.

Appropriate safeguarding measures

Different threats require different responses. An endangered weaving tradition may need apprenticeships and fair market access. An oral tradition may require recording, community-language education and opportunities for performance.

Providing resources for an annual festival may improve its continuity, but safeguarding also requires attention to the communities and knowledge systems that sustain it.

Revitalization

Revitalization involves strengthening a weakened tradition by restoring opportunities for its practice and transmission. It may include training younger participants, supporting practitioners and re-establishing relevant community activities.

It differs from attempting to freeze a tradition permanently in one historical form. Living heritage may legitimately adapt to changing circumstances.

Safeguarding traditional weaving

Displaying an old Patola textile in a museum protects a physical object. Recording weaving knowledge, supporting artisans and enabling apprentices to learn the craft contribute to safeguarding the living tradition.

Prelims focus

  • Safeguarding is concerned with the viability of living heritage.
  • Bearer communities are central to its identification and transmission.
  • Transmission can take place through formal and non-formal education.
  • Revitalization strengthens weakened cultural practices.
  • Supporting livelihoods can contribute to cultural continuity.
  • Trap: Safeguarding is not equivalent to preventing all change in a tradition.

[References: UNESCO, 2003 Convention, Articles 2(3), 14 and 15; UNESCO, Ethical Principles for Safeguarding Intangible Cultural Heritage, Principles 1, 2 and 8; NCERT, Class 11, Living Craft Traditions of India, Crafts Heritage, pp. 9–14; UNESCO, Garba of Gujarat, consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Transmission of traditional craftsmanship through apprenticeship.

title: Safeguarding, Bearer Communities and Intergenerational Transmission

body:
Documentation of living heritage

Documentation involves identifying and recording cultural practices, knowledge, associated objects and the communities responsible for maintaining them.

It helps establish what a tradition consists of, how it is transmitted, where it is practised and what threatens its continuation.

Common documentation methods

  • Written descriptions and oral-history interviews.
  • Audio recordings of songs, narratives and oral traditions.
  • Photographic and audiovisual records.
  • Documentation of craft knowledge and associated materials.
  • Community inventories, archives and digital repositories.

Inventories under the UNESCO framework

Article 12 of the 2003 Convention requires each State Party to prepare one or more inventories of intangible cultural heritage present within its territory. These inventories must be updated regularly.

Article 11 requires heritage identification and definition to involve relevant communities, groups and non-governmental organisations.

An inventory assists safeguarding by providing information about living heritage and its condition. Inclusion in a national inventory is distinct from inscription on UNESCO's international lists.

Traditional knowledge and traditional cultural expressions

ConceptMeaning
Traditional knowledgeInherited knowledge, practices, skills and understanding maintained within a community.
Traditional cultural expressionsExpressions of inherited culture, including songs, stories, designs, dances and ceremonies.
Intangible cultural heritageLiving heritage recognised and transmitted by its communities, including associated cultural objects and spaces.

These categories overlap. Traditional craft knowledge may involve skills as well as culturally significant designs. Their treatment under cultural-heritage frameworks and intellectual-property law is not identical.

Intellectual-property concerns

Intellectual-property systems generally protect specified inventions, creative works, commercial identifiers or designs under particular legal conditions.

Traditional cultural expressions are frequently developed collectively over long periods. Consequently, conventional intellectual-property rules designed around identifiable creators and particular works may not provide comprehensive protection for all inherited traditions.

Potential misuse

  • Commercial reproduction of traditional designs without appropriate recognition of their source communities.
  • Publication of sacred or restricted knowledge without permission.
  • Use of traditional songs or performances without agreed terms.
  • Unfair appropriation of economic benefits by persons outside the bearer community.

Protective approaches

ApproachPrincipal purpose
Geographical indicationProtects an eligible product's geographical identity.
Copyright and related rightsMay protect qualifying creative works, adaptations, performances and recordings.
Community access protocolsEstablish appropriate conditions for accessing cultural knowledge.
Consent and benefit-sharing arrangementsSupport agreed use and fair distribution of benefits.
Controlled documentationRecords knowledge while limiting inappropriate disclosure.

A geographical indication, commonly abbreviated as GI, identifies goods originating from a place where a given quality, reputation or other characteristic is attributable to that geographical origin. GI protection can support traditional products, but does not automatically safeguard every associated cultural practice.

Ethical documentation

UNESCO's ethical principles emphasise informed consent, community participation, respect for customary access restrictions and protection of the moral and material interests of practitioners.

Recording a tradition should not automatically result in unrestricted publication. Communities may agree to documentation while retaining restrictions on access to sacred or sensitive knowledge.

UNESCO intangible heritage inscription does not itself create copyright, patent rights, geographical indication protection or exclusive national ownership of a cultural tradition. These matters are governed by separate legal frameworks.

Prelims focus

  • Article 11 concerns national safeguarding and community participation in identification.
  • Article 12 concerns regularly updated national inventories.
  • Documentation supports safeguarding but does not replace transmission.
  • GI protection concerns geographical identity of qualifying goods.
  • Community consent and customary access restrictions are important ethical considerations.
  • Trap: UNESCO inscription does not automatically confer intellectual-property rights.

[References: UNESCO, 2003 Convention, Articles 3, 11, 12, 13 and 15; UNESCO, Ethical Principles for Safeguarding Intangible Cultural Heritage, Principles 4, 5 and 7; World Intellectual Property Organization, Documentation of Traditional Knowledge and Traditional Cultural Expressions, Background Brief No. 9, 2023, and Traditional Cultural Expressions resources, consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Consent, agreed access conditions, recognition and benefit-sharing support living heritage; restricted knowledge can remain non-public.
pictures.caption: Ethical documentation and community rights.

title: Documentation, Traditional Knowledge and Intellectual Property

body:
Adoption and purpose

UNESCO adopted the Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage on 17 October 2003. It entered into force on 20 April 2006.

India ratified the Convention on 9 September 2005.

The Convention aims to safeguard living heritage, promote respect for its practitioners, increase awareness of cultural diversity and encourage international cooperation.

Institutional structure

General Assembly

The General Assembly consists of the States Parties to the Convention. It is the Convention's sovereign body and normally meets in ordinary session every 2 years.

Intergovernmental Committee

The Intergovernmental Committee for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage oversees implementation of the Convention. It consists of representatives of 24 States Parties elected by the General Assembly.

Its responsibilities include promoting the Convention, examining nominations, maintaining the relevant international lists and considering requests for international assistance.

Important provisions

ArticleSubject
1Purposes of the Convention
2Definitions, domains and safeguarding
11Role of States Parties
12Inventories
14Education, awareness and capacity-building
15Community participation
16Representative List
17Urgent Safeguarding List
18Safeguarding programmes, projects and activities

International lists and safeguarding practices

Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity

Established under Article 16, the Representative List promotes visibility, awareness and intercultural understanding. It recognises living heritage elements without ranking the cultural value of different traditions.

Garba of Gujarat and Kumbh Mela are Indian examples.

List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding

Established under Article 17, this list concerns elements whose viability requires urgent safeguarding measures. Its purpose is to encourage action to address threats to their continuation.

Being on this list does not mean that a tradition is less valuable than one on the Representative List.

Register of Good Safeguarding Practices

Article 18 provides for the selection and promotion of programmes, projects and activities that reflect the Convention's safeguarding objectives.

The Register of Good Safeguarding Practices recognises effective safeguarding approaches rather than merely identifying individual heritage elements.

Nomination and inscription

States Parties submit nominations to UNESCO. The relevant community must participate in preparing the nomination and provide appropriate consent. The nomination is evaluated against the criteria applicable to the particular list, after which the Intergovernmental Committee takes the inscription decision.

For the Representative List, inscription criteria include conformity with the Convention's definition of intangible heritage, contribution to awareness and dialogue, safeguarding measures, community participation and consent, and inclusion in an inventory of the submitting State Party or States Parties.

International cooperation

The Convention also establishes an Intangible Cultural Heritage Fund to support its implementation and international assistance. Cooperation may involve safeguarding projects, technical support, training and exchanges of experience.

National inventory inclusion, international nomination and UNESCO inscription are separate stages. A nominated element should not be described as inscribed until the appropriate decision has been made.

Prelims focus

  • Convention adopted in 2003; entered into force in 2006.
  • India ratified it on 9 September 2005.
  • Article 16 establishes the Representative List.
  • Article 17 establishes the Urgent Safeguarding List.
  • Article 18 concerns safeguarding programmes and practices.
  • Trap: The Representative List is not a ranking of the world's most valuable cultural traditions.

[References: UNESCO, Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2003, Articles 1–8, 11–18 and 25; UNESCO, Basic Texts of the 2003 Convention and Operational Directives; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, India State Party profile, ratification record, consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The 2003 UNESCO Convention links Articles 16 and 17 to heritage lists and Article 18 to good safeguarding practices, administered by the Intergovernmental Committee.
pictures.caption: International mechanisms under the 2003 Convention.

title: UNESCO's 2003 Convention for Intangible Cultural Heritage

body:
India and UNESCO's Representative List

India possesses diverse living heritage traditions associated with religious observances, performing arts, oral knowledge, craftsmanship and community festivals.

According to UNESCO's India State Party profile consulted on 26 November 2026, India has 16 inscribed intangible cultural heritage elements, including multinational inscriptions. All 16 appear on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

Chronology of India's inscriptions

YearElementPrincipal association
2008KutiyattamSanskrit theatre of Kerala
2008Tradition of Vedic chantingOral transmission of Vedic texts
2008RamlilaTraditional performance of the Ramayana
2009RammanReligious festival and ritual theatre of Garhwal, Uttarakhand
2010Chhau danceEastern Indian dance traditions
2010Kalbelia folk songs and dancesRajasthan
2010MudiyettuRitual theatre and dance drama of Kerala
2012Buddhist chanting of LadakhRecitation of sacred Buddhist texts
2013SankirtanaRitual singing, drumming and dancing of Manipur
2014Traditional brass and copper craft of the ThatherasJandiala Guru, Punjab
2016YogaTraditional physical, mental and spiritual practices
2017Kumbh MelaReligious pilgrimage gathering
2021Durga Puja in KolkataReligious and festive traditions of West Bengal
2023Garba of GujaratDevotional and festive dance tradition
2024Nowruz or NawrouzMultinational spring and New Year tradition, extended inscription
2025DeepavaliFestival of lights

Understanding the Nowruz inscription

Nowruz is a shared cultural tradition observed in several countries. India participated in its original multinational inscription in 2009. The inscription was extended in 2016 and again in 2024.

UNESCO's current India profile records the 2024 extended inscription. The earlier and later inscriptions are stages of the same multinational element, not 3 separate Indian heritage elements.

International cultural heritage may be shared across national borders. Multinational inscription acknowledges shared traditions and does not establish exclusive ownership by any one participating country.

Important chronological distinctions

Yoga was inscribed in 2016, Kumbh Mela in 2017, Durga Puja in Kolkata in 2021 and Garba of Gujarat in 2023. These years are useful for distinguishing recent inscriptions from earlier ones.

Deepavali, inscribed in 2025, is the most recent inscribed element appearing in India's UNESCO State Party profile at the selected cutoff of 26 November 2026.

Prelims focus

  • Chhau, Kalbelia and Mudiyettu: 2010.
  • Traditional metal craft of the Thatheras: 2014.
  • Yoga: 2016; Kumbh Mela: 2017.
  • Durga Puja in Kolkata: 2021; Garba of Gujarat: 2023.
  • Deepavali: 2025.
  • Trap: Nowruz is a shared multinational element; its latest extended inscription is dated 2024.

[References: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, India State Party profile and Elements on the Lists, inscription record covering 2008–2025, consulted 26 November 2026; UNESCO Intergovernmental Committee, Decision 19.COM 7.b.56, 2024, concerning the extended Nowruz inscription.]

pictures.caption: Recent Indian intangible heritage inscriptions.
